• Adult size: about 5 cm in shell diameter
  • Lifespan: 1–2 years, depending on water temperature
  • pH: at least 7.2
  • GH: above 8 dGH
  • Peaceful scavenger that does not eat healthy plants (except duckweed and other small floating plants)

Mystery snails (Pomacea diffusa and P. bridgesii) are inexpensive and available at most pet or fish stores. Unlike pest snails such as bladder, ramshorn and Malaysian trumpet snails, they cannot self-fertilize or change sex, which makes their breeding much easier to control, and unlike their larger apple snail relatives, they won't eat your plants.

Compared to its cousins, the mystery snail or spike-topped apple snail has a pointier tip to its shell and stays smaller, at around 5 cm in diameter. The shell comes in many colours, such as golden yellow, blue, magenta, purple, ivory, chestnut brown, black and jade green, and the foot can be either light or dark.

Some hobbyists find them hardier than nerite snails, but not as good at eating algae.

One or two mystery snails can live in an aquarium of 20 litres or larger with a tight-fitting lid that prevents them from crawling out. They are safe to keep with aquarium plants but may accidentally uproot new plants in loose substrate when they crawl past them.

Although mystery snails come from South America, they cannot live in soft water. They require plenty of calcium and other minerals in their water and diet to grow a healthy, smooth shell. If you see pits and divots in the shell, try dosing mineral supplements such as Easy Shrimp and Snail Shells or Seachem Equilibrium.

  • Temperature: 21–26°C
  • pH: at least 7.2
  • GH: above 8 dGH

As with most snails, they are sensitive to salt and copper-based medications, so remove them if the aquarium is being treated with those chemicals.

As scavengers, mystery snails are not picky eaters and will eat far more than you might expect. Their diet in an aquarium usually consists of fish food, algae, biofilm, dead fish and dead plants. The one exception to the rule that they don't eat healthy plants is duckweed: there are many recorded accounts of mystery snails eating duckweed and other small floating plants, so if needed, consider putting floating plants in a floating container to protect them. If you see a snail "eating" a healthy plant, most likely it is nibbling on melted or sickly leaves.

To eat from the water surface, mystery snails can form a funnel-like shape with the foot to gather floating foods such as fish flakes. However, they usually eat off the ground or from flat surfaces.

To ensure they get plenty of minerals for strong shell growth, suitable foods include Hikari Crab Cuisine, shrimp foods, Easy Shrimp and Snail Shells, and calcium-rich vegetables such as blanched spinach or kale. An easy homemade "snello" (snail jello) food is Repashy gel food mixed with calcium powder or crushed, unflavoured calcium carbonate antacid tablets (like Tums).

These excellent scavengers clean up the aquarium by consuming excess fish food, dead animals and dead leaves so that they don't foul the water. They are very active and faster than most snails, so they will climb all over the tank.

They show fascinating behaviours, such as extending a long breathing siphon from the left shoulder. They have both gills and lungs, which allows them to breathe out of water. Holding air in the lung makes the snail float, while releasing the air makes it drop ("parasnail") to the bottom. Mystery snails can easily right themselves if they land upside down, so there is usually no need to help them.

As peaceful invertebrates, they can live with many community fish that are also compatible with higher pH and harder water. They have been kept with dwarf shrimp, tetras, kuhli loaches, corydoras, calmer betta fish that aren't very aggressive, and many other tank mates. Do not keep them with snail eaters such as puffer fish, certain loaches and turtles, and avoid any fish that may nibble on their long antennae, which look somewhat like small worms.

Sexing is difficult and takes patience and luck. Hold the snail vertically so that you look straight into the shell opening and wait for it to right itself by extending the foot; this can take 5–30 minutes or more. If the snail stretches out at the correct angle, you may see the "shoulder" regions inside the shell. Females have two holes, one over each shoulder. Males have one hole over the left shoulder, while the hole over the right shoulder is blocked by the reproductive sheath. Another technique is to watch for two snails mating: the male is the one on top. The simplest method is to buy a group of six or more snails, which gives a very high likelihood of getting both sexes.

Mystery snails do not reproduce under water; they lay their eggs above the water line to prevent predators from eating them. Each snail has a single sex and cannot change it.

Preventing breeding

  • Keep only one mystery snail per aquarium.
  • Females can store sperm for long periods, so buy a snail smaller than 2.5 cm in diameter; juveniles of that size are usually not sexually mature yet.
  • Keep the water level within 4 cm or less of the top so they have no room to lay eggs out of the water.
  • If they lay eggs on the lid or hood, remove the clutches before they hatch.

Breeding

You need at least one male and one female. To condition them, gradually increase the amount of food. Lower the water line by at least 8–10 cm from the top to give them plenty of space to lay eggs. Younger females may lay 50–100 eggs, while bigger, mature females can lay hundreds. The clutch looks like a giant, elongated pink blackberry. Use a tight-fitting lid so the eggs stay warm and humid; otherwise the egg casing hardens and dries out, preventing the babies from hatching.

Depending on temperature, the babies hatch within 1–4 weeks and look like miniature adults. They chew through the egg casing and drop into the water. Use a sponge filter or a pre-filter sponge over the intake tube so the tiny babies aren't sucked up.

Hatching the eggs separately

  1. Let the clutch harden for 1–2 days after it is laid, then gently remove it from the tank by hand.
  2. Wet one sheet of paper towel in tank water and squeeze out the excess moisture. Fold it to fit and cover the bottom of a plastic container.
  3. Place the clutch in the middle of the damp paper towel and put a couple of sheets of dry paper towel on top.
  4. Poke a few holes in the lid and close the container to maintain high humidity. Open it once a day to wipe excess moisture from the lid and replace the top paper towel if it gets too wet.
  5. When the eggs are ready to hatch, the clutch changes from pink to a mouldy, whitish-grey colour. This is normal, so do not throw it away.
  6. Place a floating breeder box in the aquarium where they will live so they get used to the water parameters. Gently rub the clutch to free the babies and break it apart. Leave the remnants in the container in case some babies have not hatched yet.

The hatchlings are very small and can be sucked up by an aquarium siphon, so keeping them in the breeder box protects them and makes feeding easier. They can eat most of the same foods as adults. After a few days you can see their colours and decide which ones to cull or give away. Once they are the size of a pea, they can be released into the main tank.

If you breed too many, you can use the techniques above to stop breeding, feed the excess to snail-eating animals, or sell some to a local fish store or other hobbyists.

If a snail has not moved for 24–48 hours, pick it up to see if it reacts; an overpowering stench means it has died. The average lifespan is 1–2 years depending on water temperature, and keeping the water on the cooler side may slow its metabolism and extend its life.
